source_terms: The most effective testimonial commercials are those which show loyal users of your product testifying to its virtues – when they don't know they are being filmed.
The interviewer pretends to find fault with the product and the loyal user rises to its defense with far more conviction than if you simply asked him what he thought of it.
The more amateurish the performance, the more credible.
item.claim: The most effective testimonial commercials show loyal users testifying when they do not know they are being filmed, and the source describes a specific device for producing conviction: the interviewer attacks the product and the user rises to its defence, which he says produces far more conviction than asking what the user thinks. He states the selection rule that follows — avoid users who would give so polished a performance that viewers would take them for professional actors, because the more amateurish the performance the more credible it is. His supporting case is a French campaign that cast an eighty-year-old laundress as its heroine; she became recognised by three in four people in France and the product is reported to have moved from fourth to second in sales.

mechanism.text: Credibility comes from the speaker appearing not to be performing for the advertiser. Defending the product against an attack, and doing it clumsily, are both signals that the speech is the speaker's own.

caveats.text: the mechanism is a claim about how sincerity is read, and the technique described — filming people who do not know they are being filmed, with an actor posing as a dealer — is a staged authenticity, which the source does not comment on

source_terms: The Law of Credentials
The crucial ingredient in the success of any brand is its claim to authenticity.
Credentials are the collateral you put up to guarantee the performance of your brand.
item.claim: Law 6. The authors start from customer disbelief: prospects are suspicious and discount most product claims. They argue one claim takes precedence over all others because it makes the others credible — the claim to authenticity, to being the real thing. Benefit claims made without credentials are, on their account, generally ignored, because every competitor makes the same sort of claim; the same benefit claims attached to a credential carry much more weight. They extend the point to buyer behaviour generally with the empty-restaurant observation: people prefer to wait for a table where there is a queue rather than eat in an empty room.

mechanism.text: Credentials work as collateral. A claim about performance is unverifiable at the point of choice, so the prospect looks for something that stands behind it; where a brand supplies that, the prospect will believe almost anything else it says. Absent it, benefit claims fall into the undifferentiated mass that provokes "that's what they all say".

scope.conditions: wherever prospects cannot verify a product claim before buying

caveats.text: 'the crucial ingredient in the success of any brand' is a universal claim demonstrated by one advertising line (Coca-Cola's 'the real thing') and two consulting cases of the authors' own
the Act and Datastream cases are the authors' own client work, reported by them with the outcome figures they chose to report and no independent source

source_terms: The family of angles causing direct reflection has grown much larger, and the range of acceptable angles for copy lighting is much smaller.
The same lighting angle that works well when the camera is farther away can cause direct reflection if the camera is closer.
item.claim: Moving the camera closer to a flat subject, with a correspondingly wider lens to keep the framing, enlarges the family of angles that produces direct reflection and shrinks the range of lighting angles that avoid it. Moving the camera farther away with a longer lens does the reverse: the family shrinks and a good lighting angle becomes easy to find. The consequence is that a lighting angle is not portable between set-ups — the same angle that was safe from a distance can produce direct reflection from close in. When the room will not allow the lights to move, the problem can sometimes be solved by moving the camera instead.

mechanism.text: The family of angles is the set of angles over all points of the surface at which a source can reflect to the camera; a closer viewpoint subtends a wider spread of those angles, so the family widens with proximity and narrows with distance.

scope.conditions: flat subjects; the source's cases are a copy stand, a museum wall with a 90-degree horizontal angle of view, and a long-lens set-up

caveats.text: extends the live family-of-angles concept (sk_lsm_c003_0013) from a fixed geometry to a variable the photographer controls; chapter 3 defines the family, this chapter makes its SIZE the operative control
supported by three lighting diagrams rather than photographs; the diagrams were not opened, so the geometry rests on the prose, which states it explicitly

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Surface Appearances', section 'Complex Surfaces'; Ch. 5, 'The Glossy Box'
item.question: A lacquered wooden gift box has to show both its high-gloss finish and the grain and colour of the wood beneath. Using this book, how do you get both in one frame, and where does the same book warn you the approach can go wrong?
item.answer: Treat it as a complex surface — one that needs both diffuse and direct reflection — and divide the surface rather than compromising across it. The authors' method is to position a source large enough to fill the entire family of angles required to produce direct reflection over the whole lid, so the gloss is available everywhere, and then block part of that source with a gobo so one region of the lid produces only diffuse reflection. In their frame the direct reflection sits camera-left and shows the gloss, and the diffusely lit camera-right region shows the grain and the true colour — and they note that the diffuse region is the only place the true colour of the wood is clearly apparent. The warning comes from the glossy-box section of the next chapter: on a three-dimensional box each visible face has its own family of angles facing a different direction, so the same large source that gives a pleasing gloss on the lid may put direct reflection on the sides too, and the ladder of geometric remedies — darker background, light toward the camera, camera height, falloff, black card on the tabletop, tipping the box, longer lens — exists for exactly that.
item.support: Ch. 4, 'Complex Surfaces', for the divided-surface method; Ch. 5, 'The Glossy Box', for the multi-face complication and the ordered remedies.
confounders: using a medium source everywhere and accepting a partial gloss, which shows neither property well
removing the direct reflection entirely to save the grain, which loses the finish
assuming the lid solution transfers unchanged to the sides, which face different directions

item.source_locator: Ch. 12, 'The Bottom of the Pyramid'; Ch. 5, 'Is There a Magic Number?'
item.question: A team proposes a cut-down free tier of a paid product for price-sensitive users, with reduced functionality and last year's model of the underlying feature set. What does this source predict, what is the alternative it points to, and how much confidence is warranted?
item.answer: It predicts the failure mode precisely and names the reason: 'What suppliers consider to be a frill, consumers consider to be a necessity.' The proposal has two components and the source objects to both. Reduced FUNCTIONALITY assumes the supplier can identify which capabilities are optional, and the source's claim is that this judgement is systematically made from the supplier's side and is systematically wrong. Last year's MODEL is the sharper error: her mechanism is that these buyers are 'aware of what is happening in the rest of the world — as it happens, in real time', so obsolescence is visible, and 'a better wood stove is not good enough in the world of LPG'. She reports that such buyers will defer a purchase to get a better product rather than settle for a far lower standard — so the cut-down tier does not capture a cheap segment, it teaches that segment to wait. THE ALTERNATIVE she points to is to reduce the UNIT rather than the PERFORMANCE: the sachet crosses a price threshold by shrinking the purchase while holding the product, and community consumption decouples use from ownership. In software terms that is usage-based or time-boxed access to the full product rather than permanent access to a degraded one. HOW MUCH CONFIDENCE IS WARRANTED: not much, and the reason is specific. The no-frills argument names no failed product anywhere — not one firm, product, date or figure — so it is a mechanism with no measured instances. It is a good reason to design the experiment differently and not a reason to believe the outcome in advance. The sachet evidence is stronger (Table 5.6 confirms rural shampoo penetration rose 13.3 to 68.7 per cent) but its attribution to unit-size innovation is the author's own footnote, not a finding, and it is a 2008 physical-goods case being carried to a digital one where unit cost behaves differently.
item.support: 'a better wood stove is not good enough in the world of LPG, nor is a black-and-white television or even a colour one without a remote'
item.confounders: The reduce-the-unit-not-the-performance rule is derived from physical goods with real marginal cost. Whether it transfers to a product whose marginal cost is near zero is a question this source cannot answer.

item.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
item.question: Freeman is careful to distinguish "close" from "close-up". What is the difference in his terms, and what common assumption about equipment does he remove?
item.answer: Close-up, he says, is to do with magnification of small things. Close is a sense of being right up against the subject, shooting from nearer than most people would consider normal and possibly nearer than feels comfortable. The assumption he removes is that close means a wide-angle lens: he says close viewpoints do not always mean wide-angle lenses, and his own example was shot at close to normal, 48mm, with tight framing doing the work instead. He also separates the practical reasons for being close — no room to stand back, obstructions such as telegraph lines forcing an architectural photographer nearer — from the expressive one, and only the expressive one carries his claim about a personal and emotional connection.
item.support: CLOSE, converted-PDF page 110. The close/close-up distinction, the 48mm figure and the separation of practical from expressive reasons are all stated there.

item.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
item.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', sections 'Show, don't tell' and 'Can you use the physical environment as your visual?' (spine 15)
item.question: Sullivan's favourite demonstration advertisement is a phone advertisement on a magazine's back cover. What makes it work on his account, and what does he say a demonstration does to the headline?
item.answer: It works by making the magazine's own front cover the evidence: the line states only that the cover photograph was shot with the advertised product's portrait mode. It is simultaneously his "show, don't tell" case and his "use the environment as the visual" case — the site of the execution is an element of the concept rather than a container for it. What a demonstration does to the headline is remove the need for a clever one: because the piece is not telling us, it did not need one. His deeper mechanism is that a demonstration is evidence rather than a claim, so it does not have to be believed on the advertiser's authority — which connects it to his argument about the collapse of authority. He gives a second case where what is shown is the cause and the reader supplies the consequence: an anti-slip skate advertisement whose mental image of children landing on their backsides he says is stronger than showing them that way.
item.support: Stated claim with two reproduced advertisements this extraction could not inspect; the argument turns on what those images do. He does not separate the force of the demonstration from the force of the placement.
confounders: reading 'show, don't tell' as a preference for imagery over copy generally
missing the second case, where the strongest version withholds the consequence rather than depicting it
assuming every product can be demonstrated; he does not claim that

item.claim: The source names two concrete opening constructions for an ad — beginning in the middle of the action, and opening on a close-up — and offers bold imagery at the start as a third means. It presents them as examples of many possible ways to earn engagement immediately, not as a required opening.

scope.conditions: Offered at the storyboard stage of an ad whose concept is already approved

caveats.text: The source hedges explicitly — "there are many ways to do this" — so these are illustrations of a principle, not a closed list and not a ranked one. No comparison between the two openings is offered.
This appears only on the Think with Google page. The Google Ads Help core table names no opening construction at all; it stops at "Jump in".

Platform- and time-contingent. This is guidance about one company's ad products on one platform. Playback behaviour, ad formats and surfaces change; the source does not claim a durable mechanism and none should be read in.

Declared publisher interest. The publisher sells advertising on the platform whose creative guidance this is, and the cited research validates that product. Third-party involvement (Ipsos as research partner; Nielsen and Kantar as independent reviewers, per the source's own account) moderates this; it does not remove it.

source_stated_remedies: Start your ad in the middle of the action, or open with a close-up

source_terms: M: There are frequently moments like these in the making of films, where huge issues of character and story are decided by the inclusion—or not—of a single shot that reverberates throughout the film.
item.claim: Murch's generalisation from a worked case: huge issues of character and story are frequently decided by whether a single shot is included, and the effect reverberates through the whole film. His case is the removal of one close-up in which a character visibly collapses on being shown evidence against his boss. With the close-up in, the other man has seen him acknowledge the truth, and everything he does for the last half-hour is done under duress — Murch's image is a metaphorical leash. With it removed, the audience sees the doubt but the other character does not, so the same subsequent actions become chosen rather than coerced. Murch says this raises the character to a level of equality with the two leads and realises the director's own stated conception of the film.

mechanism.text: What a character has been SEEN to reveal, by another character, determines whether their later behaviour reads as free or as compelled. Removing the moment of being seen removes the compulsion, without changing any subsequent shot.

scope.conditions: a shot in which one character witnesses another's exposure

caveats.text: the mechanism depends on staging as well as cutting: Murch notes the other character does not see the collapse "because of the staging of the scene", so the removal works only given how it was shot

this is the most fully worked causal argument in the chapter — one identified change, a stated mechanism, and a specific consequence traced across a named span of the film. It is also, unavoidably, a single case.

positive.description: the removal of Menzies's close-up in Touch of Evil, cutting what Murch calls the leash

intra_source_relations.note: the stated reason for the change was not the real one

provenance.section: "Night Was Night": Re-editing Touch of Evil
